questions.question: In the client-server model, what is the role of the client?
options: It stores all the data and processes business logic
It initiates requests and displays responses to the user
It routes traffic between multiple servers
It manages database connections and caching
questions.explanation: The client is the requester — it initiates communication by sending requests to the server and then presents the response to the user. Browsers, mobile apps, and CLI tools are all examples of clients.

questions.question: Which HTTP method is used to retrieve data from a server without modifying it?
options: POST
GET
PUT
DELETE
questions.explanation: GET is the HTTP method for reading data. It should be safe (no side effects) and idempotent (calling it multiple times produces the same result). Browsers use GET when you type a URL or click a link.

questions.question: What does a 404 HTTP status code indicate?
options: The server is overloaded and cannot handle the request
The request was successful and data is returned
The requested resource was not found on the server
The client is not authorized to access the resource
questions.explanation: A 404 status code means the server understood the request but cannot find the specified resource. It's one of the most common errors on the web — you've probably seen it when clicking a broken link.

questions.question: What is JSON and why is it widely used in web APIs?
options: A programming language used to build servers
A lightweight data format that is both human-readable and easy for machines to parse
A database query language similar to SQL
A security protocol for encrypting API responses
questions.explanation: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) uses simple key-value pairs and arrays to represent structured data. It's language-agnostic, lightweight, and readable by both humans and machines, making it the de facto standard for API data exchange.

questions.question: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH HTTP methods?
options: PUT creates a resource, PATCH deletes it
PUT replaces the entire resource, PATCH updates only specific fields
PUT is for files, PATCH is for database records
There is no difference — they are interchangeable
questions.explanation: PUT replaces the entire resource with the new representation sent by the client. PATCH applies a partial modification, updating only the specified fields. For example, changing just a user's email would use PATCH, while replacing the entire user object would use PUT.

questions.question: What makes an API 'RESTful'?
options: It uses WebSockets for real-time communication
It uses standard HTTP methods, stateless interactions, and resources identified by URLs
It requires authentication for every request
It only returns data in XML format
questions.explanation: REST (Representational State Transfer) is an architectural style where resources are identified by URLs, manipulated using standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), and each request is stateless — containing all information needed to process it without relying on stored session state.

questions.question: What is the difference between a 401 and a 403 HTTP status code?
options: 401 means the server is down, 403 means the request timed out
401 means not authenticated (who are you?), 403 means not authorized (you can't do that)
401 is for GET requests, 403 is for POST requests
They mean the same thing and can be used interchangeably
questions.explanation: 401 Unauthorized means the client hasn't provided valid credentials — the server doesn't know who you are. 403 Forbidden means the server knows who you are but you don't have permission to access that resource. Authentication vs. authorization.

questions.question: A developer is designing an API for a blog. Which endpoint design follows REST conventions for creating a new post?
options: GET /createPost with post data in query parameters
POST /posts with post data in the request body
PUT /newPost/create with post data in the URL
DELETE /posts/new with post data in headers
questions.explanation: RESTful design uses nouns for URLs (the resource is 'posts') and HTTP methods for actions (POST for creation). The data goes in the request body, not the URL. The server assigns an ID and typically returns 201 Created with the new resource.

questions.question: What is idempotency in the context of HTTP methods, and why does it matter?
options: It means requests are encrypted, ensuring security during transmission
It means making the same request multiple times produces the same result, which is critical for safe retries
It means the server caches every request to improve performance
It means only one client can access a resource at a time
questions.explanation: An idempotent operation yields the same result regardless of how many times it's applied. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent — retrying them safely is possible if a network failure occurs. POST is not idempotent, which is why you sometimes see 'don't click submit twice' warnings.

questions.question: When would you choose GraphQL over REST for an API, and what trade-off does it introduce?
options: GraphQL is always faster than REST and has no trade-offs
GraphQL lets clients request exactly the data they need, reducing over-fetching, but adds query complexity and caching challenges
GraphQL is only used for graph databases, REST is for everything else
GraphQL eliminates the need for a server, running entirely on the client
questions.explanation: GraphQL lets clients specify exactly which fields they want, solving REST's over-fetching and under-fetching problems. However, it introduces complexity: query parsing and validation on the server, difficulty with HTTP caching (since everything goes through POST), and potential for expensive queries that need rate limiting.
